conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had this pain in my right groin for about 12 days now. It’s pulsing, like a heartbeat, and it’s getting worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And did you notice any swelling or a lump there?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, there’s a mass. It’s tender, and I can feel it pulsing. My CT scan showed something called a pseudoaneurysm?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s right. A pseudoaneurysm is a weak spot in the artery wall. Yours is in the right external iliac artery, near where your transplant kidney used to be.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? Could it burst?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially since it’s grown to about 4 cm. That’s why we’re here—to fix it before that happens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. What’s the plan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a stent inside the artery to seal off the aneurysm. It’s a minimally invasive procedure, done through a small puncture in the groin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need surgery? I’ve had so many procedures already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No open surgery. It’s called an endovascular stent graft. We thread a catheter through the artery and place a covered stent to redirect blood flow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds better. What about my dialysis? I’m on it MWF.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do dialysis at the bedside tonight. You’re due tomorrow, and we’ll coordinate it around your procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been constipated lately too. I’ve been taking more Dilaudid for the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can definitely cause constipation. We’ll start a stool softener to help with that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. And my warfarin—I take it for my DVT. Should I keep taking it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve held it for now. Blood thinners increase bleeding risk during the procedure, so we’ll restart it after.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense. I’m also on macitentan for my pulmonary hypertension. That’s okay, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue that. It’s important for your lung pressure. We’ll keep all your other meds too, once we’re past the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been short of breath lately. Is that related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely due to your pulmonary hypertension. We’ll monitor it, but the stent shouldn’t make it worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’m a little nervous about the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s completely understandable. The team is very experienced. We’ll use imaging to guide everything in real time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the incision—will it be big?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a small puncture, about the size of a pencil lead. No stitches needed—just a bandage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. What about recovery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need to keep the leg straight for a few hours after. Then you can start moving slowly. Most patients go home in a day or two.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And dialysis? I can’t miss it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do it tomorrow morning before you’re discharged. We won’t let you miss a session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve had a lot of health issues—lupus, clotting problems, kidney failure. It’s a lot to manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing a great job managing it. We’re here to support you. Let’s get through this one step at a time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You made it through the stent procedure yesterday. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I feel okay. The groin is sore, but not as much as I expected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. The angiogram showed no blood flow into the pseudoaneurysm—so the stent is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. Can I eat now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re back on your regular diet. We also restarted your warfarin and added aspirin to protect the stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Aspirin? I thought I wasn’t supposed to take that with warfarin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: In this case, it’s necessary. The stent needs both medications to prevent clots. We’ll monitor your levels closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. My back hurts a little—can I take Tylenol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve prescribed 1000 mg as needed. Avoid NSAIDs like ibuprofen—they can affect your kidneys and increase bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And the constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve added docusate. Drink plenty of fluids and eat high-fiber foods when you can.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable, and physical therapy cleared you. You’re doing well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. Can I go home tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if your dialysis goes well tomorrow morning, you can go home in the afternoon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need follow-up with transplant surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not for this. But keep your appointment with your pulmonologist and primary care doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You finished dialysis and your vitals are stable. You’re cleared to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call if you have fever, bleeding from the groin, leg numbness, or increased pain. Elevate your leg and avoid heavy lifting for a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I can shower?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, gently. Let water run over it, then pat dry. No soaking in a tub yet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do that. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take it easy, keep up with your meds, and we’ll see you doing well at your next appointments.
